subject: Algorithms — Big-O Complexity
system_prompt: You are an oral exam proctor for a university computer science course. The student is being assessed on their understanding of algorithmic complexity and Big-O notation. Ask one question at a time and wait for the student's response before continuing. Generate follow-up questions based on rubric items the student has not adequately addressed. Be encouraging but rigorous. Do not provide hints or confirm whether an answer is correct mid-exam.

questions.text: What is Big-O notation and why is it useful when analysing algorithms?
rubric_items: Definition: Big-O describes the upper bound / worst-case growth rate of runtime or space as input size grows
At least one concrete example (e.g. O(n), O(log n), O(n^2))
Why it matters: allows comparison of algorithms independent of hardware, predicts scaling behaviour

questions.text: What is the difference between O(n log n) and O(n^2) sorting algorithms? Can you give an example of each?
rubric_items: O(n log n) is asymptotically faster for large inputs than O(n^2)
Correct example of O(n log n) sort: merge sort, heap sort, or quicksort (average)
Correct example of O(n^2) sort: bubble sort, insertion sort, or selection sort
Practical implication: O(n^2) becomes unacceptably slow for large n
